description:
Ruddy Duck (Oxyura jamaicensis) – female & male

Image 1: female
Image 2: male & female
Images 3-4: female

13 February 2016 
Village Creek Drying Beds 
NW Green Oaks Boulevard/N. Fielder Road 
Arlington, Texas

Hundreds if not thousands of ducks and other waterfowl were observed at the site of the Village Creek Drying Beds. They very slowly but surely tend to gently swim away as one approaches on the high berms or lower hiking paths available. A few other folks were out there with their scopes and cameras, another with a set of binoculars and a dog. A single Turkey Vulture flew overhead making high and low turns as it were. Song Sparrows, Red-winged Blackbirds, and Yellow-rumped Warblers were observed on the wooded side opposite the collection of ponds. The ponds were all filled with water and some of them poured over their respective dividing land spaces and thus joined due to the abundance of the liquid. Bonaparte's Gulls, American Coots, Gadwalls, and Northern Shovelers were the most common waterfowl on site with lesser numbers of other species including Ruddy Duck. The hike around the perimeter of the Village Creek Drying Beds makes for good exercise; it is easily a two-to-three mile loop.

Among the many North American bird and duck species that breed in the northern reaches of the continent (Canada mainly, and usually Alaska to a greater or lesser extent), one of these has about equal breeding ranges in both the most western states of the US West and Midwest and the Western and Central provinces of Canada, and that duck is Ruddy Duck (Oxyura jamaicensis). At the same time Ruddy Duck shares extensive permanent range in areas of the US West from New Mexico to California and north to Oregon. But this is one of the stiff-tailed duck species that claims a relatively greater portion of its permanent range in Mexico than the United States. Similarly, Ruddy Duck is extensively found on a permanent basis throughout the Caribbean nations. Ruddy Duck is a nonbreeding resident and/or migratory flier through all of Texas including the North Texas region where we made this observation. In Mexico, where Ruddy Duck does not have a permanent presence it is a nonbreeding resident during winter and except for the Yucatán Peninsula, it occurs throughout the nation. Ruddy Duck’s wintering range extends south to Central America as far as the northwestern Pacific Coast of Nicaragua. Ruddy Duck does not reach or extend its range into South America. Because of its extensive range throughout North America, Ruddy Duck is an authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere. The Village Creek Drying Beds are administered by the City of Arlington, Texas.

"Ruddy ducks are native to North and South America. These stiff-tailed ducks nest in western and central Canada and much of the western United States as far east as the Great Lakes region and south to central Texas, throughout Baja California, and to the transvolcanic belt in Mexico. Wintering range extends throughout most of southern North America, from California through the Great Lakes region and the Atlantic coast south of southern Maine to as far south as western Guatemala and El Salvador. Ruddy ducks were introduced to England in 1960 in Gloucestershire. From there these ducks have colonized Ireland and Belgium. Ruddy ducks introduced in Europe are migratory birds from the eastern United States and Mexico. Two subspecies including Oxyura jamaicensis ferruginea and Oxura jamaicensis andina can be found in the West Indies, Columbia, and throughout the Andes Mountains. description:
This Ruddy Duck is most likely a female. The morphology of ruddy ducks varies between sexes as well as seasonally. During the summer male ruddy ducks have rich chestnut necks and bodies. The crown, nape, and tail, which are held erect or horizontal to the water, are dark brown. Males have pure white faces, whereas females have a dark line across the face. Females and juveniles have barred bodies that lack any chesnut coloring. During the winter, male ruddy ducks resemble females. Their pure white face remains the primary distinguishing characteristic. Ruddy ducks have large, spatulate, pale blue bills. Males tend to be larger than females in weight and wingspan. Males are 142 to 154 mm from wing tip to wing tip and weigh from 540 to 795 g. Females are 135 to 149 mm from wing tip to wing tip and weigh 310 to 650 g. Body length is from 35 to 43 cm.

Male ruddy ducks have two molts. The prenuptial molt occurs in the summer months and reveals a plumage that is similar to that of females. The postnuptial molt occurs from August to October and reveals their winter plumage of bright chestnut. During this time the bill becomes bright blue as well. (Gooders and Boyer, 1986; Kortright, 1967)

Ruddy ducks have large, spatulate, pale blue bills. Males tend to be larger than females in weight and wingspan. Males are 142 to 154 mm from wing tip to wing tip and weigh from 540 to 795 g. Females are 135 to 149 mm from wing tip to wing tip and weigh 310 to 650 g. Body length is from 35 to 43 cm.

Male ruddy ducks have two molts. The prenuptial molt occurs in the summer months and reveals a plumage that is similar to that of females. The postnuptial molt occurs from August to October and reveals their winter plumage of bright chestnut. During this time the bill becomes bright blue as well. Ruddy Duck (Oxyura jamaicensis)

Usual size: anywhere from 13-17" (average is 15"), with a wingspan of 18-19". 

Significant Appearance(s): Black head with white cheeks and dark blueish bill. Back feathers are dark brown with less dark body feathers. Tail is long and usually seen pointing upward.

Other facts: Usually nest near marshy vegetation on lakes and ponds; primarily feeds on seeds and roots of aquatic plants, aquatic insects, and crustaceans. Interesting fact - Due to its build, ruddy ducks can barely walk on land.

Waterfowl/Birds seen in vicinity: Canada Goose (Branta canadensis) approximately 50+/-, Tundra Swan (Larus argentatus)approximately 30+/-; Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) approximately 40+/-, and a Red Tail Hawk (Buteo jamaicensis) also flying overhead in the area.

Ruddy Duck (Oxyura jamaicensis) is a small, migratory duck in the Typical Stifftails (Oxyura) Genus. The stiff tail feathers serve as a rudder for this diving duck. They are rarely seen on land. Ruddy Duck is a "small, compact duck with a long, stiff, fan-shaped tail that is raised when in display. Breeding males have a chestnut body, black cap, white cheek, and a broad, baby-blue bill. Winter males have a brown body, black cap and white cheek. Females and immature males are brown overall with a dark cap and blurry dark line through the cheek. The weather at the start was post-sunset, 54 degrees ("feels like" 51), and breezy (NW at 10 mph). By the time we arrived, only three gulls remained on the lake, but the Franklin's was one of them We left at 1736 and headed to Panera Bread in Clearwater for the North Pinellas CBC countdown.

The other one of three.
